summary: Suggests several updates to the Reliable Data Protocol specified in RFC 908, based on experience. This revised version is experimental.

eli5.summary: A way to send messages that makes sure they all arrive. This is a newer, improved version based on what people learned.

subtitle: Fixes to the Reliable Data Protocol: a new checksum, 16-bit ports and a list of corrected ambiguities.

tldr.problem: Experiments in 1986 and 1987 turned up ambiguities and problems in the Reliable Data Protocol (RDP) specification in RFC 908.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1151 changes the header (the TCP checksum, 16-bit ports, version number 2) and corrects a list of errors in RFC 908's pseudo-code and text.
tldr.outcome: The revised protocol is experimental, and the authors say the demand for RDP implementations was limited.

today: RFC 1151 updates RFC 908 and is experimental. The unit metadata shows no later RFC replacing it.

sections.title: Why a Version 2
sections.content:
Experiments in 1986 and 1987 found ambiguities and problems in the RDP specification (RFC 908). The authors hoped to revise the whole specification, but given the limited demand for RDP implementations they could not justify the time. This memo instead lists the changes they believe are appropriate to RDP version 1.

Readers are expected to know RFC 908. The memo is marked experimental.
sections.eli5: People tried the first rule book and found confusing spots, so the authors wrote a short list of fixes instead of a whole new book.

sections.title: Changes to the Header
sections.content:
Three things change in the header. The checksum algorithm is replaced: the cost of the old RDP checksum was surprisingly variable, and optimized implementations on two comparable hardware bases differed in performance by a factor of five. RDP now uses the 16-bit TCP checksum specified on page 16 of RFC 793.

The port size grows from 8 to 16 bits. Port numbers below 1024 are reserved for well-defined applications, and allocable ports begin at 1024. Because both changed, the version number is now 2.

The header begins with the flag bits SYN, ACK, EAK, RST and NUL, then the version number and header length, followed by the source port, destination port, data length, sequence number, acknowledgement number and checksum, and then a variable header area.
sections.eli5: The address numbers were made bigger so more programs fit, the error check was swapped for one that is quicker to compute, and the version sticker was changed to 2.

sections.title: Corrected Errors in RFC 908
sections.content:
Several errors are fixed. SND.UNA must always be set to SEG.ACK+1. The SYN-SENT pseudo-code should test the ACK bit after the other tests, and in the SYN-RCVD state the local peer should deallocate the connection record and close instead of being left half-open. In the CLOSED state, a reset for non-data packets should use SEG.SEG because RCV.CUR is not defined there.

A RST in the CLOSE-WAIT state should leave the connection in CLOSE-WAIT. An acknowledgement of in-sequence data may include EACKs. The right edge of the window is outside the window, so the total window size is 2*X, where X is the maximum number of outstanding segments.
sections.eli5: It is a list of spots where the first instructions disagreed with themselves, with the answer for each one.

sections.title: An Open Flow-Control Problem
sections.content:
RDP's flow control does not let the receiver close the sender's window. If the receiver acknowledges segments as they arrive, the sender can easily send more data than the receiver can buffer.

A fix suggested by members of the End-2-End Research Group is to acknowledge a segment only after it has been delivered to the application. The memo says this scheme has not been tested. The memo also states that security issues are not addressed.
sections.eli5: The receiver could not tell the sender to slow down. One idea is to only say thanks after you have actually used what was sent, but nobody had tried it.

references.text: Transmission Control Protocol, RFC 793 (checksum on page 16).
